name: Home UVB booth

card.summary: A stand-up narrowband UVB phototherapy cabinet meant for home skin treatment; it is a medical light device, and its use for cosmetic tanning has not been studied.
card.aka: Home phototherapy booth, home NB-UVB cabinet
card.note: UV radiation is classed as a Group 1 carcinogen by the IARC; contraindications include photosensitising drugs and herbs.

quick.overview:
A home UVB booth is a full-body cabinet that emits narrowband ultraviolet-B light, typically around 311-313 nm. Dermatology uses this wavelength to treat conditions such as psoriasis, vitiligo and eczema, and some patients receive treatment at home instead of in a clinic.

In looksmaxxing and tanning circles the booth comes up as a way to darken skin using mostly UVB rather than the UVA-heavy light of salon sunbeds. Published research on these devices concerns skin disease, not cosmetic tanning, so there are no trials of a home UVB booth as a tanning tool.
quick.mechanism: Narrowband UVB acts on skin cells and the immune system in the treated areas, which is why it is used for inflammatory and pigment disorders. UVB also stimulates new melanin production over a few days, whereas UVA mainly darkens melanin already present. Salon sunbeds emit mostly UVA with a small UVB share, so a UVB-dominant booth differs from them in spectrum.
quick.risks: UV exposure is associated with progressive skin damage, skin cancer, cataracts and burns, and the IARC classifies UV radiation as a Group 1 carcinogen. Photosensitising drugs, some herbs (such as St John's wort), porphyria and photosensitive skin conditions are listed as contraindications to phototherapy. Medical use is normally supervised by a clinician, and rules on tanning devices vary by country.

lead: A home UVB booth is a stand-up cabinet fitted with narrowband ultraviolet-B (NB-UVB) lamps, designed so that a person can receive whole-body phototherapy at home instead of attending a clinic. Narrowband UVB emits around 311-313 nanometres and is the most widely used form of phototherapy in dermatology [1]. A large, high-power UVB booth can deliver full-body treatment at home as an alternative to office-based treatment [1].

The booth's established uses are medical. Phototherapy is used for psoriasis, atopic dermatitis, vitiligo and several other skin conditions [1][3][4][5]. A randomised equivalence trial published in 2024 compared home-based and office-based NB-UVB for psoriasis [5]. Researchers have not published trials of a home UVB booth as a cosmetic tanning device.

In appearance communities the booth appears as a tanning idea: because UVB triggers new melanin production while UVA mostly darkens existing pigment, some users see a UVB-rich unit as a different route to a tan from a salon sunbed [2]. Public health bodies and researchers point out that UV radiation is a recognised carcinogen and that indoor tanning is associated with higher melanoma risk [2].

paras: Phototherapy units for skin disease range from small handheld lamps to full-body cabinets. A booth of the kind discussed here is a vertical enclosure lined with narrowband UVB tubes, with exposure lasting seconds to minutes depending on lamp intensity and the person's skin sensitivity [1]. Narrowband UVB sits at roughly 311-313 nm, a slice of the UVB range (about 280-315 nm) that dermatologists favour for therapy [1][2].

Wikipedia notes that full-body UVB treatment can be given either at a doctor's office or at home with a large, high-power UVB booth [1]. The home option has been tested against office treatment in a randomised trial in psoriasis [5].

Narrowband UVB is an established treatment for psoriasis and is used for atopic dermatitis, vitiligo, polymorphous light eruption, some cutaneous lymphomas and lichen planus [1]. A 2017 systematic review and meta-analysis in JAMA Dermatology pooled prospective studies of phototherapy for generalised vitiligo, including 1201 patients treated with narrowband UVB, to estimate expected repigmentation [3]. A 2024 American Academy of Dermatology guideline makes conditional recommendations in favour of phototherapy for adults with atopic dermatitis who do not respond to topical treatment, while making strong recommendations for several biologic and JAK-inhibitor drugs [4].

Systematic reviews of treatments for pityriasis lichenoides report that most studies used UV phototherapy, including narrowband UVB, with clearance rates of roughly 70-100% across modalities that are hard to compare directly [6]. Network meta-analyses of systemic treatments for atopic dermatitis and chronic urticaria have included phototherapy among the interventions assessed [7][8]. These conditions are medical; none of this research addresses tanning.
The LITE trial, published in JAMA Dermatology in 2024, was a multicentre, pragmatic randomised equivalence trial comparing home-based with office-based narrowband UVB for patients with psoriasis [5].

Indoor tanning devices differ in spectrum. According to Wikipedia, modern salon beds emit no UVC, a small amount of UVB and mostly UVA, and the beds developed by Friedrich Wolff in the 1970s produced roughly 95% UVA and 5% UVB [2]. UVA produces a quick tan by darkening melanin already in the skin, while UVB triggers new melanin production over about 72 hours, which gives a longer-lasting tan; UVB is also the band most associated with burning [2].

Users on the T Nation forum have discussed this difference. One 2005 thread advises asking a salon about a booth's UVB percentage and says that the lowest-UVB booths are the most expensive and allegedly give the deepest tan with the least burning [9]. A 2008 thread states that getting a 'base tan' in a booth to avoid burning in the sun is a myth because beds emit proportionally less UVB than the sun [10]. Neither claim is backed by controlled studies in the sources reviewed here.

Wikipedia reports that UV exposure causes progressive skin damage and redness even at small doses and is linked to DNA and collagen damage, cataracts and skin cancer [1]. Contraindications to phototherapy include photosensitising drugs or herbs such as St John's wort, photosensitive skin disease and porphyria, with caution advised for drugs such as methotrexate and chloroquine [1].

For tanning, the WHO's International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies UV radiation as a Group 1 carcinogen [2]. A 2012 meta-analysis by Boniol and colleagues found a relative risk of melanoma of 1.20 for ever-users of tanning devices and 1.59 for those who began before age 35 [2]. A 2014 meta-analysis by Wehner and colleagues estimated that indoor tanning causes more than 10,000 melanoma cases and about 450,000 non-melanoma skin cancers annually [2]. These figures concern salon tanning devices and not home UVB booths specifically.

The Danish-Faroese physician Niels Finsen developed an artificial ultraviolet light source for treating skin disease in the 1890s and received the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine [1][2]. Home 'sunlamps' marketed in the 1920s emitted a large share of UVB and often caused burns [2]. Friedrich Wolff invented the modern UVA-dominant sunbed in 1975 and tanning devices reached the US market in 1978 [2]. In the United States the FDA reclassified tanning beds from low risk to moderate risk in 2014 [2].

Rules on tanning devices differ by country. Brazil banned cosmetic use of tanning beds in 2009, Australia banned commercial tanning in 2015 while leaving private ownership legal, and France banned minors from indoor tanning in 1997 [2]. In the US the FDA requires a warning against use by under-18s and many states restrict minors [2]. These rules address tanning beds; home phototherapy cabinets are medical devices used under clinical supervision.
No studies found on home UVB booths as a cosmetic tanning device.

Related research covers medical phototherapy. A 2017 meta-analysis assessed narrowband UVB and PUVA for vitiligo [3]; a 2024 guideline addresses phototherapy for adult atopic dermatitis [4]; a 2024 randomised trial compared home with office NB-UVB for psoriasis [5]; and systematic reviews have examined phototherapy for pityriasis lichenoides and, within network meta-analyses, for chronic urticaria [6][8]. Phototherapy has also been studied for neonatal jaundice using different light sources and wavelengths [11].

lore.intro: On gym and fitness forums the home UVB booth is mentioned mainly in tanning threads, where members trade ideas about which light spectrum tans most deeply with the least burning [9][10].

claims.claim: Booths with a low UVB percentage give the deepest tan with the least burning.
claims.believers: A T Nation poster says to ask a salon about a booth's UVB percentage, that the lowest-UVB booths cost the most, and that they allegedly give the deepest tan with the least potential for burning [9].
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes UVA as producing a quick tan by darkening existing melanin and UVB as causing both burning and new melanin production [2]. No published trial compares the tan produced by different booth spectra.

claims.claim: A 'base tan' from a booth is said to give limited protection against burning outdoors.
claims.believers: A 2008 T Nation poster says that tanning beds emit proportionally less UVB than the sun and that people with a 'base tan' can still burn badly outdoors [10].
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes that indoor tanning beds emit mostly UVA and that UV radiation as a whole is a Group 1 carcinogen [2]. The sources reviewed contain no trial testing whether a booth tan reduces later sunburn.
